summary: This informational RFC evaluates the Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL) using simulations of a small outdoor sensor deployment and a large smart meter network, reporting several routing performance metrics.

eli5.summary: It tests how well a message-passing system for tiny sensors works, in a computer simulation of two real setups.

questions: rpl simulation results for smart meter networks
how does rpl perform in large networks
what are rpl path quality metrics
how much control traffic does rpl use
subtitle: Simulation results for RPL routing in low-power networks

tldr.problem: RPL is a routing protocol designed for low-power, lossy networks, but operators need to understand its real-world performance in practical scenarios before deployment.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC presents a discrete-event simulation of RPL on two topologies: a 45-node outdoor sensor network and a 2442-node smart meter network, using real link quality traces to measure routing performance, control overhead, delay, and recovery from failures.
tldr.outcome: The simulations show RPL achieves near-optimal path quality with negligible control overhead, meets delay requirements for industrial and building automation use cases, and scales well to thousands of nodes.

today: RFC 6687 is an Informational document presenting simulation results for RPL performance evaluation. It has not been obsoleted and remains a key reference for understanding RPL behavior in realistic deployments, though operators should also consult RFC 6550 and applicability statements for their specific use case.

sections.title: Testing RPL with Realistic Data
sections.content:
RPL, the Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks, was standardized in RFC 6550 to handle the unique challenges of low-power devices connected by unreliable (lossy) wireless links. Examples include home automation, industrial sensor networks, and smart metering systems. Before operators deploy it, they need confidence in its performance.

Simulation is a practical way to test routing protocols at scale. This RFC uses a discrete-event simulator (OMNeT++) running a complete RPL implementation with real-world network topologies and link quality traces collected from actual deployments. The authors measure path quality, control plane overhead, end-to-end delay, routing table sizes, and recovery time after failures.

The simulation covers two scenarios: a small outdoor sensor deployment (45 nodes) and a large smart meter network (2442 nodes). Results show how RPL performs under different traffic patterns, failure rates, and parameter settings.
sections.eli5: A team built a computer model of a tiny-device network, fed it real data from actual deployments, and watched how RPL handled routing. They checked if the protocol was fast, light on overhead, and reliable.

sections.title: Simulation Setup and Methodology
sections.content:
The simulation uses OMNeT++ with the Castalia framework for wireless sensor networks. Two key aspects of the simulation are realistic:

Real Link Quality. Rather than assuming a theoretical loss model, the authors derived link failure patterns from actual network traces recorded during real deployments. Each link in the simulation has a time-varying Packet Delivery Ratio (PDR) that changes every 10 minutes in the simulation, reflecting real conditions where some links are strong, some weak, and some highly variable.

Real Topologies. The 45-node outdoor network comes from a real sensor deployment. The 2442-node network is a real smart meter installation. Using real topologies avoids the bias of random topology generators.

In the simulations, RPL builds a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) rooted at an LLN Border Router (LBR). The protocol uses trickle timers to control how often nodes send DIO (Destination Information Object) and DAO (Destination Advertisement Object) control messages. Nodes use the ETX (Expected Transmission Count) metric to evaluate link quality and select parents.
sections.eli5: The researchers used actual maps of real networks and actual records of how well each link worked on real days, then plugged that data into the simulator so the test would be realistic.

sections.title: Path Quality and Routing Performance
sections.content:
For the 45-node outdoor deployment, path quality is evaluated by comparing RPL's routes to hypothetical ideal shortest-path routing (the best possible routes). The results show that 90% of packets travel at most 5 hops via RPL versus 4 hops via ideal routing—a small penalty. In terms of ETX cost (total expected transmissions), 90% of packets via RPL have ETX cost of 4.87 or less, compared to 4 for ideal routing.

The protocol achieves this near-optimal performance while maintaining small routing tables: 90% of nodes store fewer than 10 entries, critical for memory-constrained devices.

In the larger smart meter network (2442 nodes), RPL's path cost is within 30% of ideal shortest-path routing on average. The protocol is non-optimal because it intentionally avoids switching parents when the improvement is less than 20%, trading path quality for stability and lower control overhead.

An important finding: RPL provides loose bounds on end-to-end delay. For the 45-node network with up to 7 hops, about 99% of packets are delivered within 100 ms, meeting industrial automation requirements. For the smart meter network with traffic every 30 seconds, end-to-end latency is typically 500 ms to 1 second.
sections.eli5: RPL's paths were almost as good as the best possible paths, and packets arrived quickly enough for real-world use. It used very little memory on each device too.

sections.title: Control Plane Overhead and Stability
sections.content:
One of RPL's key features is its use of trickle timers to suppress redundant control messages. Results show control traffic is negligible compared to data traffic—even for nodes close to the root handling most of the data, control packets are a small fraction of total traffic.

The control overhead exhibits a saw-tooth pattern: as the network stabilizes under steady conditions, DIOs are sent less frequently (trickle interval increases). When topology changes occur (link failures, PDR changes) or when the root issues a new DAG sequence number, timers reset and control traffic spikes briefly, then drops again.

Increasing the frequency of global repair (how often the root issues new DAG sequence numbers) reduces control overhead but increases periods of lost connectivity after a failure. Conversely, enabling local repair (nodes locally 'poison' broken routes and recompute quickly) restores connectivity in seconds at minimal extra overhead. The simulation shows that with local repair, 85% of nodes regain connectivity within seconds, versus 150+ seconds without it.

In the large smart meter network, maximum control load is about 2000 packets per minute at the most-loaded node, while data traffic is much higher, confirming RPL scales well.
sections.eli5: RPL is very quiet most of the time (not many control messages). When something breaks, it talks more to fix it, but only briefly. Adding a quick local repair mechanism lets it recover fast without being chatty.

sections.title: Performance in Different Scenarios
sections.content:
Building Automation. When 60% of traffic targets neighbors (1 hop away) and 20% targets 2-hop nodes, RPL's P2P paths are much closer to ideal. Path latency for 1- to 2-hop distances stays below 60 ms for 99% of packets, suitable for real-time home automation.

Large-Scale Smart Meter Networks. In the 2442-node network with all traffic destined to the root (upstream only), RPL handles the uniform traffic pattern well. End-to-end latency averages 500 ms to 1 second, acceptable for meter reading applications that tolerate seconds of delay.

Stability vs. Optimality Trade-Off. When the implementation tolerates a 0% cost change before switching parents, 95% of paths are within 10% of ideal cost, but control overhead increases. With a 20% tolerance, 95% of paths are within 20% of ideal cost, and control overhead drops significantly. Operators can tune this trade-off for their application.
sections.eli5: RPL works well for different jobs: when devices talk to close neighbors, it's fast and accurate. For meter reading (everyone talking to one hub), it's slow but reliable. You can dial up accuracy or dial up stability depending on your needs.
